title: Book 7, Chapter 23 — Nineteenth Year of the War—Battles in the Great Harbour—Retreat and Annihilation of the Athenian Army
paragraphs: While the Athenians lingered on like this without moving from where they were, Gylippus and Sicanus arrived at Syracuse. Sicanus had failed to win Agrigentum, the party friendly to the Syracusans having been driven out while he was still at Gela; but Gylippus came accompanied not only by a large number of troops raised in Sicily, but also by the heavy infantry sent off in spring from the Peloponnese in the merchant ships, who had reached Selinus from Libya. They had been carried to Libya by a storm, and after obtaining two galleys and pilots from the Cyrenians, on their voyage along the coast had taken the side of the Euesperitae and defeated the Libyans who were besieging them. From there, coasting on to Neapolis, a Carthaginian trading post and the nearest point to Sicily — only two days’ and a night’s voyage away — they had crossed over and reached Selinus. As soon as they arrived, the Syracusans prepared to attack the Athenians again by land and sea at once. The Athenian generals, seeing a fresh army come to the enemy’s aid, and that their own situation, far from improving, was getting worse by the day — and above all distressed by the sickness of the soldiers — now began to regret not having pulled out earlier; and Nicias, no longer offering the same opposition, except to urge that there should be no open vote, gave orders as secretly as possible for everyone to be ready to sail out from camp at a given signal. All was finally ready, and they were on the point of sailing away, when an eclipse of the moon, which was then full, occurred. Most of the Athenians, deeply impressed by it, urged the generals to wait; and Nicias, who was somewhat over-addicted to divination and that sort of thing, refused from that moment even to consider the question of departure until they had waited the thrice nine days prescribed by the soothsayers.

The besiegers were thus forced to stay in the country, and the Syracusans, getting wind of what had happened, became more eager than ever to press the Athenians, who had now themselves admitted they were no longer their superiors either by sea or by land — otherwise they would never have planned to sail away. Besides, the Syracusans did not want them to settle in any other part of Sicily, where they would be harder to deal with, but wanted to force them to fight at sea as quickly as possible, in a position favourable to themselves. Accordingly they manned their ships and trained for as many days as they thought necessary. When the moment came, they assaulted the Athenian lines on the first day, and when a small force of heavy infantry and horse came out against them by certain gates, they cut off some of the infantry, routed and chased them back to the lines, where, since the entrance was narrow, the Athenians lost seventy horses and a few of their heavy infantry.

After drawing off their troops for that day, the Syracusans on the next went out with a fleet of seventy-six ships, and at the same time advanced with their land forces against the lines. The Athenians put out to meet them with eighty-six ships, came to close quarters, and engaged. The Syracusans and their allies first defeated the Athenian centre, and then caught Eurymedon, the commander of the right wing, who was sailing out from the line more towards the land in order to surround the enemy, in the hollow recess of the harbour, killed him, and destroyed the ships with him; after which they chased the whole Athenian fleet before them and drove it ashore.

Gylippus, seeing the enemy’s fleet defeated and driven ashore beyond their stockades and camp, ran down to the breakwater with some of his troops, in order to cut off the men as they landed and make it easier for the Syracusans to tow off the ships, the shore being friendly ground. The Tyrrhenians who guarded this point for the Athenians, seeing them coming on in disorder, advanced out against them, attacked and routed their van, and hurled it into the marsh of Lysimeleia. Afterwards the Syracusan and allied troops arrived in greater numbers, and the Athenians, fearing for their ships, also came up to the rescue, engaged them, and defeated and pursued them some distance, killing a few of their heavy infantry. They succeeded in saving most of their ships and brought them down by their camp; but eighteen were taken by the Syracusans and their allies, and all the men killed. The rest the enemy tried to burn by means of an old merchant ship which they filled with faggots and pine-wood, set on fire, and let drift down the wind that blew full on the Athenians. The Athenians, however, alarmed for their ships, contrived means to stop and put it out, checking the flames and the closer approach of the merchant ship, and so escaped the danger.

After this the Syracusans set up a trophy for the sea-fight and for the heavy infantry they had cut off up at the lines, where they had taken the horses; and the Athenians for the rout of the foot driven by the Tyrrhenians into the marsh, and for their own victory with the rest of the army.

The Syracusans had now won a decisive victory at sea, where until now they had feared the reinforcement brought by Demosthenes; and deep, in consequence, was the despondency of the Athenians, and great their disappointment, and greater still their regret for ever having come on the expedition. These were the only cities they had so far encountered that were similar in character to their own, under democracies like themselves, with ships, horses, and considerable size. They had been unable to divide them and bring them over by holding out the prospect of changes in their governments, or to crush them by their great superiority in force; they had failed in most of their attempts, and being already in difficulty, had now been defeated at sea where defeat could never have been expected, and were thus plunged deeper in trouble than ever.

Meanwhile the Syracusans immediately began to sail freely along the harbour, and resolved to close up its mouth, so that the Athenians could not slip out in future even if they wished. Indeed, the Syracusans no longer thought only of saving themselves, but also of how to prevent the enemy from escaping. They thought, and rightly, that they were now much the stronger, and that to defeat the Athenians and their allies by land and sea would win them great glory in Hellas. The rest of the Hellenes would thus be either freed at once or released from fear, since the remaining forces of Athens would no longer be able to sustain the war that would be waged against her; while they, the Syracusans, would be regarded as the authors of this deliverance and held in high admiration, both by all men now living and by posterity. Nor were these the only considerations that lent dignity to the struggle. They would thus conquer not only the Athenians but also their numerous allies, and conquer not alone but with their fellow combatants, commanding side by side with the Corinthians and Lacedaemonians, having offered their city to stand in the front of danger and having been in great measure the pioneers of naval success.

Indeed, there were never so many peoples assembled before a single city, if we leave aside the grand total brought together in this war under Athens and Lacedaemon. The following were the states on either side that came to Syracuse to fight for or against Sicily, to help to conquer or defend the island. Right or community of blood was not so much the bond of union among them as interest or compulsion, depending on the case. The Athenians themselves, being Ionians, went against the Dorians of Syracuse of their own free will; and the peoples still speaking Attic and using the Athenian laws — the Lemnians, Imbrians, and Aeginetans, that is, the then occupants of Aegina, being their colonists — went with them. To these must be added the Hestiaeans living at Hestiaea in Euboea. Of the rest, some joined the expedition as Athenian subjects, others as independent allies, others as mercenaries. Among the tribute-paying subjects were the Eretrians, Chalcidians, Styrians, and Carystians from Euboea; the Ceans, Andrians, and Tenians from the islands; and the Milesians, Samians, and Chians from Ionia. The Chians, however, joined as independent allies, paying no tribute, but providing ships. Most of these were Ionians and descended from the Athenians, except the Carystians, who are Dryopes, and although subjects and obliged to serve, were still Ionians fighting against Dorians. Besides these, there were men of Aeolian race — the Methymnians, subjects who provided ships, not tribute, and the Tenedians and Aenians who paid tribute. These Aeolians fought against their Aeolian founders, the Boeotians in the Syracusan army, because they were obliged to, while the Plataeans, the only native Boeotians opposed to Boeotians, did so on a just quarrel. Of the Rhodians and Cytherians, both Dorians, the latter, Lacedaemonian colonists, fought in the Athenian ranks against their Lacedaemonian countrymen with Gylippus; while the Rhodians, Argive by race, were forced to bear arms against the Dorian Syracusans and against their own colonists, the Geloans, serving with the Syracusans. Of the islanders round the Peloponnese, the Cephallenians and Zacynthians accompanied the Athenians as independent allies, although their insular position really left them little choice, given the maritime supremacy of Athens; while the Corcyraeans, who were not only Dorians but Corinthians, were openly serving against Corinthians and Syracusans, although colonists of the former and of the same race as the latter, under colour of compulsion but really out of free will, through hatred of Corinth. The Messenians, as they are now called in Naupactus and from Pylos, then held by the Athenians, were taken with them to the war. There were also a few Megarian exiles, whose fate it was now to be fighting against the Megarian Selinuntines.

The participation of the rest was more voluntary in nature. It was less the league than hatred of the Lacedaemonians and the immediate private advantage of each individual that persuaded the Dorian Argives to join the Ionian Athenians in a war against Dorians; while the Mantineans and other Arcadian mercenaries, used to going against whatever enemy was pointed out to them, were led by interest to regard the Arcadians serving with the Corinthians as just as much their enemies as anyone else. The Cretans and Aetolians also served for hire; and the Cretans, who had joined the Rhodians in founding Gela, thus came to consent to fight for pay against, instead of for, their colonists. There were also some Acarnanians paid to serve, although they came chiefly out of love for Demosthenes and goodwill toward the Athenians, whose allies they were. These all lived on the Hellenic side of the Ionian Gulf. Of the Italiots, there were the Thurians and Metapontines, dragged into the quarrel by the harsh necessities of a time of revolution; of the Siceliots, the Naxians and the Catanians; and of the barbarians, the Egestaeans, who had called in the Athenians, most of the Sicels, and outside Sicily some Tyrrhenian enemies of Syracuse and Iapygian mercenaries.

Such were the peoples serving with the Athenians. Against these the Syracusans had the Camarinaeans, their neighbours, and the Geloans, who live next to them; then, passing over the neutral Agrigentines, the Selinuntines settled on the far side of the island. These inhabit the part of Sicily looking toward Libya; the Himeraeans came from the side toward the Tyrrhenian Sea, being the only Hellenic inhabitants in that quarter, and the only people who came from there to help the Syracusans. Of the Hellenes in Sicily, the above peoples joined the war, all Dorians and independent; and of the barbarians, the Sicels only — those, that is, who did not go over to the Athenians. Of the Hellenes outside Sicily there were the Lacedaemonians, who provided a Spartan to take command, along with a force of Neodamodes (or Freedmen) and Helots; the Corinthians, the only people who joined with both naval and land forces, with their Leucadian and Ambraciot kinsmen; some mercenaries sent by Corinth from Arcadia; some Sicyonians forced to serve; and from outside the Peloponnese, the Boeotians. In comparison, however, with these foreign auxiliaries, the great Siceliot cities provided more in every department — heavy infantry, ships, and horses in numbers, and an immense crowd besides; while in comparison again, one may say, with all the rest put together, more was provided by the Syracusans themselves, both because of the size of the city and because they were in the greatest danger.

Such were the auxiliaries brought together on either side, all of which had by now joined, neither party gaining any further additions afterwards. It was no wonder, then, if the Syracusans and their allies thought it would win them great glory if they could follow up their recent victory in the sea-fight by capturing the whole Athenian armada, without letting it escape either by sea or by land. They began at once to close up the Great Harbour by means of boats, merchant ships, and galleys moored broadside across its mouth, which is nearly a mile wide, and made all their other arrangements for the case that the Athenians might venture to fight at sea again. There was, in fact, nothing small either in their plans or in their ideas.

The Athenians, seeing them closing up the harbour and informed of their further plans, called a council of war. The generals and colonels assembled and discussed the difficulties of the situation. The most pressing point was that they no longer had provisions for immediate use (having sent on to Catana to tell them not to send any, in the belief that they were leaving), and would not have any in future unless they could control the sea. They therefore decided to evacuate their upper lines, to enclose with a cross wall and garrison a small space close to the ships, just enough to hold their stores and sick, and, manning all the ships, seaworthy or not, with every man that could be spared from the rest of their land forces, to fight it out at sea, and, if victorious, to go to Catana, or, if not, to burn their ships, form in close order, and retreat by land for the nearest friendly place they could reach, Hellenic or barbarian. This was no sooner decided than carried into effect: they came down gradually from the upper lines and manned all their ships, forcing on board everyone of age to be of any use. They thus succeeded in manning about one hundred and ten ships in all, on which they embarked a number of archers and darters from the Acarnanians and the other foreigners, making all other arrangements that the nature of their plan and the necessities forced on them allowed. All was now nearly ready, and Nicias, seeing the soldiers disheartened by their unprecedented and decisive defeat at sea, and eager because of the shortage of provisions to fight it out as soon as possible, called them all together and addressed them first, speaking as follows:

“Soldiers of Athens and of the allies, we all have an equal stake in the coming struggle, in which life and country are at stake for us as much as they are for the enemy; for if our fleet wins the day, each man can see his native city again, wherever that city may be. You must not lose heart or be like men with no experience, who fail in a first attempt and ever after fearfully predict a future as disastrous. Let the Athenians among you who have already had experience of many wars, and the allies who have joined us in so many expeditions, remember the surprises of war, and, with the hope that fortune will not be always against us, prepare to fight again in a manner worthy of the numbers you see yourselves to be.

“Now, whatever we thought would be of service against the crush of vessels in such a narrow harbour, and against the troops on the enemy’s decks, from which we suffered before, has all been considered with the helmsmen and, as far as our means allowed, provided. A number of archers and darters will go on board, and a multitude we should not have used in an action in the open sea, where our skill would be hampered by the weight of the vessels; but in the present land-fight that we are forced to make from shipboard, all this will be useful. We have also worked out the changes in construction we must make to meet theirs; and against the thickness of their cheeks, which did us the greatest damage, we have provided grappling-irons, which will prevent an attacker from backing water after charging, if the soldiers on deck here do their duty; for we are absolutely compelled to fight a land battle from the fleet, and it seems to be in our interest neither to back water ourselves nor to let the enemy do so, especially as the shore, except so much of it as may be held by our troops, is hostile ground.

“You must remember this and fight on as long as you can, and must not let yourselves be driven ashore; once alongside the enemy, you must make up your minds not to part company until you have swept the heavy infantry from his deck. I say this more for the heavy infantry than for the seamen, since it is more the business of the men on deck; and our land forces are even now, on the whole, the strongest. The sailors I advise, and at the same time implore, not to be too daunted by their misfortunes, now that we have our decks better armed and a greater number of vessels. Bear in mind how well worth preserving is the pleasure felt by those of you who, through your knowledge of our language and imitation of our manners, have always been considered Athenians, even though not so in fact, and as such have been honoured throughout Hellas, and have had your full share of the advantages of our empire, and more than your share of the respect of our subjects and of protection from ill-treatment. You, with whom alone we share our empire freely, we now justly require not to betray that empire in its extremity. In contempt of the Corinthians, whom you have often defeated, and of the Siceliots, none of whom so much as presumed to stand against us when our navy was in its prime, we ask you to repel them, and to show that even in sickness and disaster your skill is more than a match for the fortune and vigour of any other.

“For the Athenians among you, I add this reflection once more: you left no more such ships in your docks as these, no more heavy infantry in their flower; if you do anything but conquer, our enemies here will sail there at once, and those of us left at Athens will be unable to repel their home assailants reinforced by these new allies. Here you will fall at once into the hands of the Syracusans — I need not remind you of the intentions with which you attacked them — and your countrymen at home will fall into those of the Lacedaemonians. Since the fate of both thus hangs on this single battle, now if ever stand firm, and remember, each and all, that you who are now going on board are the army and navy of the Athenians, and all that is left of the state and of the great name of Athens. In her defence, if any man has any advantage in skill or courage, now is the time for him to show it, and so serve himself and save all.”

After this address Nicias at once gave orders to man the ships. Meanwhile Gylippus and the Syracusans could see by the preparations going on that the Athenians meant to fight at sea. They had also had notice of the grappling-irons, against which they took special precautions by stretching hides over the prows and much of the upper part of their ships, so that the irons, when thrown, might slip off without taking hold. With everything now ready, the generals and Gylippus addressed them as follows:

“Syracusans and allies, the glorious character of our past achievements, and the no less glorious results at stake in the coming battle, are, we think, understood by most of you, or you would never have thrown yourselves with such ardour into the struggle; and if there is anyone not as fully aware of the facts as he should be, we will state them for him. The Athenians came to this country first to conquer Sicily, and after that, if successful, the Peloponnese and the rest of Hellas, already possessing the greatest empire ever known among the Hellenes, of present or former times. Here, for the first time, they found in you men who faced the navy that had made them masters everywhere; you have already defeated them in the previous sea-fights, and will in all likelihood defeat them again now. When men are once checked in what they consider their special excellence, their whole opinion of themselves suffers more than if they had not first believed in their superiority, the unexpected shock to their pride causing them to give way more than their real strength warrants; and this is probably the case with the Athenians now.

“With us it is different. The original estimate of ourselves that gave us courage in the days of our unskilfulness has been strengthened, while the conviction added to it — that we must be the best seamen of the age, since we have beaten the best — has given a double measure of hope to every man among us; and, for the most part, where there is the greatest hope, there is also the greatest ardour for action. The means they have tried to find against us by copying our equipment are familiar to our way of fighting, and will be met with proper provisions, while they will never be able to have a number of heavy infantry on their decks, contrary to their custom, and a number of darters (born landsmen, one might say — Acarnanians and others — embarked afloat, who will not know how to discharge their weapons when they have to keep still) without hampering their ships and falling all into confusion among themselves through fighting outside their own tactics. They will gain nothing by the number of their ships — I say this to those of you who may be alarmed at having to fight against odds — since a quantity of ships in a confined space will only be slower in carrying out the manoeuvres required, and most exposed to damage from our means of attack. Indeed, if you would know the plain truth, as we are credibly informed, the excess of their sufferings and the necessities of their present distress have made them desperate; they have no confidence in their force, but want to try their fortune in the only way they can, and either to force their passage and sail out, or after this to retreat by land, since it is impossible for them to be worse off than they are.

“The fortune of our greatest enemies having thus betrayed itself, and their disorder being what I have described, let us engage in anger, convinced that, as between adversaries, nothing is more legitimate than to claim the right to sate the whole wrath of one’s soul in punishing the aggressor, and that nothing, as the proverb has it, is sweeter than vengeance on an enemy — which it will now be ours to take. That they are enemies, and mortal enemies, you all know, since they came here to enslave our country, and if successful had in store for our men everything that is most dreadful, for our children and wives everything most dishonourable, and for the whole city the name that conveys the greatest reproach. None should therefore relent, or think it gain if they go away without further danger to us. They will do that just the same, even if they win; while if we succeed, as we may expect, in punishing them, and in handing down to all Sicily her ancient freedom, strengthened and confirmed, we shall have achieved no mean triumph. And the rarest dangers are those in which failure brings little loss and success the greatest gain.”

After this address to their soldiers, the Syracusan generals and Gylippus saw that the Athenians were manning their ships and immediately proceeded to man their own. Meanwhile Nicias, appalled by the position of affairs and realizing the greatness and the nearness of the danger now that they were on the point of putting out from shore, and thinking, as men are apt to in great crises, that when all has been done they still have something left to do, and that when all has been said they have not yet said enough, again called on the captains one by one. He addressed each by his father’s name and his own, and by that of his tribe, and adjured them not to belie their personal renown or to obscure the hereditary virtues for which their ancestors were illustrious. He reminded them of their country, the freest of the free, and of the unrestricted discretion it allowed each man to live as he pleased; and he added other arguments such as men use at such a moment, and which, with little alteration, are made to serve on all such occasions — appeals to wives, children, and national gods — without caring whether they are thought commonplace, but loudly invoking them in the belief that they will help in the consternation of the moment. Having admonished them, not as he wished but as he could, Nicias withdrew and led the troops to the sea, ranging them in as long a line as he was able, in order to do all he could to sustain the courage of the men afloat. Demosthenes, Menander, and Euthydemus, who took the command on board, then put out from their own camp and sailed straight for the barrier across the mouth of the harbour and the passage left open, to try to force their way out.

The Syracusans and their allies had already put out with about the same number of ships as before, part of which kept guard at the outlet, while the rest were stationed all round the rest of the harbour to attack the Athenians on every side at once; while the land forces held themselves ready at the points where the ships might run ashore. The Syracusan fleet was commanded by Sicanus and Agatharchus, who each had a wing of the whole force, with Pythen and the Corinthians in the centre. When the Athenians came up to the barrier, with the first shock of their charge they overpowered the ships stationed there and tried to undo the fastenings; after this, as the Syracusans and their allies bore down on them from every quarter, the action spread from the barrier over the whole harbour, and was more obstinately disputed than any of the previous engagements. On either side the rowers showed great zeal in bringing up their ships at the boatswains’ orders; the helmsmen great skill in manoeuvring, and great rivalry with each other; and the ships once alongside, the soldiers on board did their best not to let the work on deck be outdone by the others. In short, every man strove to prove himself first in his particular department. As many ships were engaged in a small space — for these were the largest fleets ever known to fight in the narrowest space, being together a little short of two hundred — the regular attacks with the beak were few, since there was no chance of backing water or of breaking the line; while the collisions caused by one ship chancing to run foul of another, either fleeing from or attacking a third, were more frequent. As long as a ship was coming up to the charge, the men on the decks rained darts, arrows, and stones on her; but once alongside, the heavy infantry tried to board each other’s ship, fighting hand to hand. In many quarters it happened, because of the cramped space, that a ship was charging an enemy on one side and being charged herself on another, and that two or sometimes more ships had got entangled around one, forcing the helmsmen to attend to defence here, offence there — not to one thing at a time, but to many on every side; while the huge din caused by the number of ships crashing together not only spread terror but made the orders of the boatswains inaudible. The boatswains on either side, in the discharge of their duty and in the heat of the conflict, shouted orders and appeals to their men incessantly. The Athenians they urged to force the passage out, and now if ever to show their mettle and lay hold of a safe return to their country; the Syracusans and their allies they cried that it would be glorious to prevent the escape of the enemy, and, conquering, to exalt the countries that were theirs. The generals, moreover, on either side, if they saw any ship in any part of the battle backing ashore without being forced to do so, called out to the captain by name and asked him — the Athenians, whether they were retreating because they thought the thrice-hostile shore more their own than that sea which had cost them so much labour to win; the Syracusans, whether they were running from the running Athenians, whom they well knew to be eager to escape any way they could.

Meanwhile the two armies on shore, while victory hung in the balance, were a prey to the most agonizing and conflicting emotions. The natives thirsted for more glory than they had already won; the invaders feared finding themselves in even worse plight than before. Since the all of the Athenians was set upon their fleet, their fear for the outcome was like nothing they had ever felt; while their view of the struggle was necessarily as varied as the battle itself. Close to the action and not all looking at the same point at once, some saw their friends winning and took heart, calling on heaven not to deprive them of safety; while others, with their eyes turned on the losers, wailed and cried aloud, and, although mere spectators, were more overcome than the actual combatants. Others again were gazing at some spot where the battle was evenly disputed; as the strife was prolonged without decision, their swaying bodies reflected the agitation of their minds, and they suffered the worst agony of all, ever just within reach of safety or just on the point of destruction. In short, in that one Athenian army, as long as the sea-fight remained doubtful, every sound was to be heard at once — shrieks, cheers, “We win,” “We lose,” and all the other cries that a great host would necessarily utter in great peril; and with the men in the fleet it was nearly the same. Until at last the Syracusans and their allies, after the battle had lasted a long while, put the Athenians to flight, and with much shouting and cheering chased them in open rout to the shore. The naval force, one one way, one another, all those not taken afloat now ran ashore and rushed from on board to their camp; while the army, no longer divided but carried away by one impulse, all with shrieks and groans deplored what had happened, and ran down — some to help the ships, others to guard what was left of their wall, while the largest part already began to consider how they should save themselves. Indeed, the panic of that moment had never been surpassed. They now suffered very nearly what they had inflicted at Pylos: as then the Lacedaemonians with the loss of their fleet had also lost the men who had crossed over to the island, so now the Athenians had no hope of escaping by land, without the help of some extraordinary accident.

The sea-fight having been a hard one, with many ships and lives lost on both sides, the victorious Syracusans and their allies now picked up their wrecks and dead and sailed off to the city, where they set up a trophy. The Athenians, overwhelmed by their disaster, did not even think of asking leave to take up their dead or wrecks, but wanted to retreat that very night. Demosthenes, however, went to Nicias and gave it as his opinion that they should man the ships they had left and make another effort to force their way out the next morning, saying that they still had more ships fit for service than the enemy — the Athenians having about sixty remaining as against less than fifty of their opponents. Nicias was entirely of his mind; but when they wished to man the ships, the sailors refused to go on board, being so utterly overwhelmed by their defeat that they no longer believed in the possibility of success.

Accordingly, they all now made up their minds to retreat by land. Meanwhile the Syracusan Hermocrates — suspecting their intention, and impressed by the danger of allowing a force of that size to retire by land, settle in some other part of Sicily, and from there renew the war — went and stated his views to the authorities, pointing out that they ought not to let the enemy get away by night, but that all the Syracusans and their allies should at once march out, block up the roads, and seize and guard the passes. The authorities entirely agreed with him and thought it ought to be done, but on the other hand felt sure that the people, who had given themselves over to celebration and were taking their ease after a great battle at sea, would not be easily brought to obey; besides, they were celebrating a festival, having on that day a sacrifice to Heracles, and most of them in their joy at the victory had fallen to drinking at the festival, and would probably consent to anything sooner than to take up their arms and march out at that moment. For these reasons, the thing seemed impracticable to the magistrates; and Hermocrates, finding himself unable to do anything further with them, now resorted to a stratagem of his own. What he feared was that the Athenians might quietly get the start of them by passing the most difficult places during the night; and so, as soon as it was dusk, he sent some friends of his own to the camp with some horsemen who rode up within earshot and called out to some of the men, as though they were well-wishers of the Athenians, telling them to tell Nicias (who in fact had some correspondents who informed him of what went on inside the town) not to lead the army off by night, since the Syracusans were guarding the roads, but to make his preparations at his leisure and to retreat by day. After saying this, they departed; and their hearers informed the Athenian generals, who, on the strength of this message, put off going for that night, not doubting its sincerity.

Since after all they had not set out at once, they now decided to stay also the next day, to give time to the soldiers to pack up as well as they could the most useful articles, and, leaving everything else behind, to start only with what was strictly necessary for their personal subsistence. Meanwhile the Syracusans and Gylippus marched out and blocked up the roads through the country by which the Athenians were likely to pass, and kept guard at the fords of the streams and rivers, posting themselves so as to receive them and stop the army wherever they thought best; while their fleet sailed up to the beach and towed off the Athenian ships. Some few were burnt by the Athenians themselves as they had intended; the rest the Syracusans lashed onto their own at their leisure as they had been thrown up on shore, without anyone trying to stop them, and conveyed to the town.

After this, with Nicias and Demosthenes thinking that enough had been done by way of preparation, the army moved off on the second day after the sea-fight. It was a lamentable scene, not merely in the single fact that they were retreating after losing all their ships, with their great hopes gone and themselves and the state in peril; but also in the things, on leaving the camp, that were most grievous for every eye and heart to look upon. The dead lay unburied, and each man, as he recognized a friend among them, shuddered with grief and horror; while the living whom they were leaving behind, wounded or sick, were to the living far more shocking than the dead, and more to be pitied than those who had perished. These fell to entreating and bewailing until their friends did not know what to do, begging them to take them, loudly calling each individual comrade or relative they could see, hanging on the necks of their tent-fellows in the act of departure, and following as far as they could; and, when their bodily strength failed them, calling again and again on heaven and shrieking aloud as they were left behind. So that the whole army, filled with tears and distracted in this fashion, found it not easy to set out, even from an enemy’s land where they had already suffered evils too great for tears, and from the unknown future before them feared to suffer more. Dejection and self-condemnation were also rife among them. Indeed they could only be compared to a starved-out town, and that no small one, escaping; the whole multitude on the march being not less than forty thousand men. All carried anything they could that might be of use; and the heavy infantry and cavalry, contrary to their custom, while under arms carried their own provisions, in some cases for want of servants, in others through not trusting them — they had long been deserting and now did so in greater numbers than ever. Yet even so they did not carry enough, since there was no longer food in the camp. Moreover, their disgrace generally, and the universality of their sufferings, however somewhat alleviated by being borne in company, were still felt at the moment to be a heavy burden — especially when they contrasted the splendour and glory of their setting out with the humiliation in which it had ended. For this was by far the greatest reverse that ever befell a Hellenic army. They had come to enslave others, and were leaving in fear of being enslaved themselves; they had sailed out with prayer and paeans, and now started back with omens directly contrary, travelling by land instead of by sea, and trusting not in their fleet but in their heavy infantry. Nevertheless, the greatness of the danger still hanging over them made all this seem tolerable.

Nicias, seeing the army dejected and greatly altered, passed along the ranks and encouraged and comforted them as far as was possible under the circumstances, raising his voice still higher and higher as he went from one company to another, in his earnestness and his anxiety that the benefit of his words might reach as many as possible:

“Athenians and allies, even in our present position we must still hope on, since men have before now been saved from worse straits than this; and you must not condemn yourselves too severely either for your disasters or for your present unmerited sufferings. I myself, who am no stronger than any of you — indeed you see how I am with my sickness — and who in the gifts of fortune am, I think, in private life or otherwise, the equal of any, am now exposed to the same danger as the meanest among you; and yet my life has been one of much devotion to the gods, and of much justice and without offence toward men. I have therefore still a strong hope for the future, and our misfortunes do not terrify me as much as they might. Indeed, we may hope that they will be lightened: our enemies have had good fortune enough; and if any of the gods was offended at our expedition, we have already been amply punished. Others before us have attacked their neighbours and have done what men will do without suffering more than they could bear; and we may now justly expect to find the gods more kind, since we have become fitter objects of their pity than of their jealousy. Then look at yourselves, mark the numbers and quality of the heavy infantry marching in your ranks, and do not give way too much to despondency. Reflect that you are yourselves at once a city wherever you sit down, and that there is no other in Sicily that could easily resist your attack, or expel you when once established. The safety and order of the march is for yourselves to look to; the one thought of each man being that the spot where he may be forced to fight must be conquered and held as his country and stronghold. Meanwhile we shall hasten on our way night and day alike, since our provisions are scanty; and if we can reach some friendly place of the Sicels — whom fear of the Syracusans still keeps loyal to us — you may then consider yourselves safe. A message has been sent on to them with directions to meet us with supplies of food. To sum up, be convinced, soldiers, that you must be brave, since there is no place near for your cowardice to take refuge in; and that if you now escape from the enemy, you may all see again what your hearts desire, while those of you who are Athenians will raise up again the great power of the state, fallen though it is. Men make the city, and not walls or ships without men in them.”

As he made this address, Nicias went along the ranks and brought back to their place any of the troops he saw straggling out of the line; while Demosthenes did the same for his part of the army, addressing them in very similar words. The army marched in a hollow square, with the division under Nicias leading and that of Demosthenes following, the heavy infantry on the outside, and the baggage-carriers and the bulk of the army in the middle. When they reached the ford of the river Anapus, they found drawn up there a body of Syracusans and allies; routing these, they made good their passage and pushed on, harassed by the charges of the Syracusan horse and by the missiles of their light troops. On that day they advanced about four and a half miles, halting for the night on a certain hill. The next day they started early and got on about two miles further, and descended into a place in the plain and there encamped, in order to procure some food from the houses, since the place was inhabited, and to carry water with them from there, since for many furlongs ahead, in the direction in which they were going, it was not plentiful. The Syracusans meanwhile went on and fortified the pass in front, where there was a steep hill with a rocky ravine on each side, called the Acraean cliff. The next day the Athenians, advancing, found themselves hindered by the missiles and charges of the horse and darters, both very numerous, of the Syracusans and allies; and after fighting for a long while, they at length retired to the same camp, where they no longer had provisions as before, since it was impossible to leave their position because of the cavalry.

Early next morning they started again and forced their way to the hill, which had been fortified, where they found before them the enemy’s infantry drawn up many shields deep to defend the fortification, the pass being narrow. The Athenians assaulted the work but were greeted by a storm of missiles from the hill, which told with the greater effect because it was steep; unable to force the passage, they retreated again and rested. Meanwhile some claps of thunder and rain occurred, as often happens towards autumn, which still further disheartened the Athenians, who thought all these things to be omens of their approaching ruin. While they were resting, Gylippus and the Syracusans sent part of their army to throw up works in their rear on the way they had advanced; but the Athenians immediately sent some of their own men and prevented them; after which they retreated more towards the plain and halted for the night. When they advanced the next day, the Syracusans surrounded and attacked them on every side, disabling many, falling back if the Athenians advanced and coming on if they retreated, and in particular assaulting their rear, in the hope of routing them in detail and so striking a panic into the whole army. For a long while the Athenians persevered in this fashion, but after advancing for four or five furlongs they halted to rest in the plain, the Syracusans also withdrawing to their own camp.

During the night Nicias and Demosthenes, seeing the wretched condition of their troops, now in want of every kind of necessary, and large numbers disabled in the many attacks of the enemy, decided to light as many fires as possible, and to lead the army off, no longer by the same route they had intended, but towards the sea in the opposite direction to the one guarded by the Syracusans. The whole of this route was leading the army not to Catana but to the other side of Sicily, towards Camarina, Gela, and the other Hellenic and barbarian towns in that quarter. They accordingly lit a number of fires and set out by night. Now all armies, and the largest most of all, are liable to fears and alarms, especially when marching by night through enemy country and with the enemy near; and the Athenians falling into one of these panics, the leading division, that of Nicias, kept together and got on a good way in front, while that of Demosthenes, comprising rather more than half the army, got separated and marched on in some disorder. By morning, however, they reached the sea, and getting onto the Helorine road, pushed on in order to reach the river Cacyparis and to follow the stream up through the interior, where they hoped to be met by the Sicels they had sent for. Arrived at the river, they found there too a Syracusan party engaged in barring the passage of the ford with a wall and a palisade; forcing this guard, they crossed the river and went on to another, called the Erineus, on the advice of their guides.

Meanwhile, when day came and the Syracusans and allies found that the Athenians were gone, most of them accused Gylippus of having let them escape on purpose, and hastily pursuing by the road which they had no difficulty in finding the Athenians had taken, overtook them about dinner-time. They first came up with the troops under Demosthenes, who were behind and marching somewhat slowly and in disorder, owing to the night panic mentioned above, and at once attacked and engaged them, the Syracusan horse surrounding them with more ease now that they were separated from the rest, and hemming them in on one spot. The division of Nicias was five or six miles further on in front, since he led them more rapidly, thinking that under the circumstances their safety lay not in staying and fighting unless obliged, but in retreating as fast as possible, and only fighting when forced to. Demosthenes, on the other hand, was generally speaking harassed more incessantly, since his post in the rear left him the first exposed to the attacks of the enemy. Now, finding that the Syracusans were in pursuit, he stopped pushing on, in order to form his men for battle, and so lingered until he was surrounded by his pursuers, and he and the Athenians with him were placed in the most distressing position, huddled into an enclosure with a wall all round it, a road on this side and on that, and olive trees in great numbers, where missiles were showered in upon them from every quarter. This mode of attack the Syracusans had with good reason adopted in preference to fighting at close quarters, since to risk a struggle with desperate men was now more to the Athenians’ advantage than to their own; besides, their success had now become so certain that they began to spare themselves a little so as not to be cut off in the moment of victory, thinking too that, even as it was, they would be able in this way to subdue and capture the enemy.

In fact, after plying the Athenians and their allies all day long with missiles from every side, they at last saw they were worn out with their wounds and other sufferings; and Gylippus and the Syracusans and their allies made a proclamation, offering their liberty to any of the islanders who chose to come over to them; and a few cities went over. Afterwards a capitulation was agreed upon for all the rest with Demosthenes, to lay down their arms on condition that no one was to be put to death either by violence, imprisonment, or want of the necessaries of life. On these terms they surrendered to the number of six thousand in all, laying down all the money they had, which filled the hollows of four shields, and were immediately conveyed by the Syracusans to the town.

Meanwhile Nicias with his division reached the river Erineus that day, crossed over, and posted his army on some high ground on the other side. The next day the Syracusans overtook him and told him that the troops under Demosthenes had surrendered, and invited him to follow their example. Incredulous, Nicias asked for a truce to send a horseman to see; and on the messenger’s return with the news that they had indeed surrendered, sent a herald to Gylippus and the Syracusans, saying that he was prepared to agree, on behalf of the Athenians, to repay whatever money the Syracusans had spent on the war if they would let his army go; and offered, until the money was paid, to give Athenians as hostages, one for every talent. The Syracusans and Gylippus rejected this proposal, and attacked this division as they had the other, standing all round and plying them with missiles until evening. Food and necessaries were as miserably wanting to the troops of Nicias as they had been to their comrades; nevertheless they watched for the quiet of the night to resume their march. But as they were taking up their arms, the Syracusans noticed it and raised their paean, at which the Athenians, finding they were discovered, laid down their arms again, except for about three hundred men who forced their way through the guards and went on during the night as they were able.

As soon as it was day, Nicias put his army in motion, pressed, as before, by the Syracusans and their allies, pelted from every side by their missiles and struck down by their javelins. The Athenians pushed on for the Assinarus, urged by the attacks made on them from every side by a numerous cavalry and the swarm of other arms, fancying that they would breathe more freely once across the river, and driven on too by their exhaustion and craving for water. Once there they rushed in, and all order was at an end, every man wanting to cross first; and the attacks of the enemy made it difficult to cross at all. Forced to huddle together, they fell against and trod down one another, some dying immediately on the javelins, others getting entangled and stumbling over the baggage, unable to rise again. Meanwhile the opposite bank, which was steep, was lined by the Syracusans, who showered missiles down on the Athenians, most of whom were drinking greedily and heaped together in disorder in the hollow bed of the river. The Peloponnesians also came down and butchered them, especially those in the water, which was thus immediately spoiled, but which they went on drinking just the same — mud and all, bloody as it was — most even fighting to have it.

At last, when many dead now lay piled one on another in the stream, and part of the army had been destroyed at the river, and the few who had escaped from there were cut off by the cavalry, Nicias surrendered himself to Gylippus, whom he trusted more than the Syracusans, and told him and the Lacedaemonians to do what they liked with him, but to stop the slaughter of the soldiers. Gylippus, after this, immediately gave orders to take prisoners, on which the rest were brought together alive, except for a large number secreted by the soldiery; and a party was sent in pursuit of the three hundred who had got through the guard during the night, and who were now taken with the rest. The number of the enemy collected as public property was not considerable, but that secreted was very large, and all Sicily was filled with them, no convention having been made in their case as in the case of those taken with Demosthenes. Besides this, a large portion were killed outright, the carnage being very great, and not exceeded by any in this Sicilian war. In the numerous other engagements on the march, not a few had also fallen. Nevertheless many escaped, some at the moment, others after serving as slaves and then running away later. These found refuge at Catana.

The Syracusans and their allies now mustered, took up the spoils and as many prisoners as they could, and went back to the city. The rest of their Athenian and allied captives were deposited in the quarries, this seeming the safest way of keeping them; but Nicias and Demosthenes were butchered, against the will of Gylippus, who thought it would be the crown of his triumph if he could take the enemy’s generals to Lacedaemon. One of them, as it happened — Demosthenes — was one of her greatest enemies, on account of the affair of the island and of Pylos; while the other, Nicias, was for the same reasons one of her greatest friends, owing to his exertions to procure the release of the prisoners by persuading the Athenians to make peace. For these reasons the Lacedaemonians felt kindly towards him, and it was on this that Nicias himself mainly relied when he surrendered to Gylippus. But some of the Syracusans who had been in correspondence with him were afraid, it was said, that he would be put to the torture and trouble their success by his revelations; others, especially the Corinthians, that he might escape — being wealthy — by means of bribes, and live to do them further mischief. These persuaded the allies and put him to death. This, or something like it, was the cause of the death of a man who, of all the Hellenes in my time, least deserved such a fate, seeing that the whole course of his life had been regulated with strict attention to virtue.

The prisoners in the quarries were at first hardly treated by the Syracusans. Crowded into a narrow hole, with no roof to cover them, they were tormented during the day by the heat of the sun and the stifling closeness of the air; and then the nights, which came on autumnal and chilly, made them ill from the violence of the change. Besides, since they had to do everything in the same place for want of room, and the bodies of those who died of their wounds, of the change in temperature, or of similar causes, were left heaped together one upon another, intolerable stenches arose; while hunger and thirst never stopped tormenting them, each man during eight months being given only half a pint of water and a pint of corn a day. In short, no single suffering to be expected for men thrust into such a place was spared them. For about seventy days they thus lived all together, after which all but the Athenians and any Siceliots or Italiots who had joined the expedition were sold. The total number of prisoners taken would be difficult to state exactly, but it cannot have been less than seven thousand.

This was the greatest Hellenic achievement of any in this war, or, in my opinion, in Hellenic history; at once most glorious to the victors and most calamitous to the conquered. They were beaten at all points and altogether; everything they suffered was great; they were destroyed, as the saying is, with a total destruction; their fleet, their army, everything was destroyed; and few out of many returned home. Such were the events in Sicily.
